rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention window will guide narrower gradients and targeted slope or temperature changes.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. The short scouting retention times leave room for this diagnostic run without a substantial time penalty.
The shallower gradient resolved most of the cluster but left one near-coelution. Raising temperature at the same slope tests thermal selectivity for that pair and should shorten retention.

Test an intermediate temperature to separate the near-coelution seen at 40 C without compressing the middle pair as strongly as at 55 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates this selectivity tradeoff.

Make the gradient modestly shallower at the best-performing temperature to test whether the remaining close pair can reach full resolution. If this pushes the last peak beyond 10 minutes, a higher starting organic fraction can then recover time.

The middle pair appears to cross between 45 and 55 C, so moving to 60 C may increase its separation while also improving the late pair. Return to the 20-minute gradient to keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

At 60 C, the previously limiting middle pair is resolved, but a later pair has become critical. A slightly steeper gradient should move that later pair away from its apparent convergence while testing whether the middle pair retains sufficient resolution.

Slightly reduce the slope to improve the middle pair that narrowly missed baseline resolution. This probes the narrow tradeoff between that pair and the later pair while keeping the last peak well below 10 minutes.

Keep the slope of injection 7 but raise the starting organic fraction to shift selectivity and shorten retention. This tests whether the narrowly deficient middle pair can improve without sacrificing the later pair.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to improve both crowded middle pairs, taking advantage of the extra separation gained in the later pair. The endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window, and the last peak should stay below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the marginal middle pairs above R = 1.5 while preserving the later pair's remaining margin. The endpoint is still above the last peak's elution window, with retention expected below 10 minutes.

Injection 11 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to seek a shorter fully resolved separation while compensating for compression of the middle pairs.

The higher starting fraction lost resolution, so retain injection 11 as the maximum-score benchmark. Test a cooler selectivity regime at its gradient settings to look for larger resolution margins that could support subsequent acceleration.

Test whether further cooling separates the remaining close pair in the low-temperature regime while retaining resolution elsewhere. Injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this run explores an alternative selectivity window.

Test a shallower gradient at 25 C to improve the remaining close pair, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the longer retention. Injection 11 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score benchmark.

Continue narrowing the gradient window at 25 C: the previous step improved the limiting pair and shortened retention. This tests whether that trend reaches full resolution, with injection 11 retained as the maximum-score benchmark.

Combine modest warming with a slightly shallower gradient to improve the stubborn middle pair while preserving separation from its earlier neighbor. The warmer temperature should help offset the retention increase from the shallower slope; injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to 25 C while retaining the shallower slope to test whether the limiting middle pair from injection 16 reaches full resolution. This isolates temperature from injection 17; injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the solvent window while preserving injection 18's slope to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature separation. Its resolution margins provide room to test this acceleration, while injection 11 remains the fastest maximum-score method observed.

Reduce the slope at injection 19's starting fraction to recover the middle-pair resolution lost when shifting the solvent window. This may yield another fully resolved method below 10 minutes, while injection 11 remains the fastest maximum-score benchmark.

Test a one-step shorter gradient around injection 11, the fastest maximum-score method. This directly checks the acceleration limit; if critical pairs fall below R = 1.5, retain the 10-minute gradient as the benchmark.

The shorter gradient lost resolution, so retain injection 11 as the fastest maximum-score method. Test a shallower slope at the higher starting fraction to recover injection 12's limiting middle pair while checking whether the later pair remains resolved.

Test a shorter programmed gradient with a narrower solvent window, keeping its slope close to the fully resolved injection 11. This checks whether the later critical pair tolerates the slight slope reduction; injection 11 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Probe a slope of 0.04444 organic fraction per minute, between injections 11 and 23, to refine the fully resolved operating boundary. Injection 11 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the preferred method unless this run offers a useful resolution margin.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower slope than injection 8, seeking full resolution in the low-starting-organic window. Injection 11 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the preferred, fastest fully resolved method unless this run improves that result.
